modelAnswer: Enthalpy (H) is the total amount of thermal energy stored in a compound.

explain.title: The system and its surrounding
explain.body: In Chemistry, any physical or chemical change under study may also be called a system. The chemical reaction includes reactants, products, catalyst, solvent and anything else which is important to study this reaction. Everything else which does not fall in this system is called the surrounding. In the beaker example, the water is the system and the beaker and burner are in the surrounding.

explain.title: Energy entering or leaving
explain.body: When energy is transferred from surrounding to the system, the change is called endothermic and it has a positive sign. When energy is transferred from system to surrounding, the change is called exothermic and it carries a negative sign. The surroundings get cooler when they supply energy and warmer when they receive energy.

explain.title: Enthalpy and heat
explain.body: Enthalpy (H) or heat content, is defined as the total amount of thermal energy stored in a compound. The unit of its measurement is kJ mol⁻¹. Energy absorbed during a reaction increases the total enthalpy of the system; energy evolved during a reaction decreases it.

mistakes: Do not call everything in the experiment the system; the system is the part or change being studied.
Do not reverse the direction: endothermic energy goes from the surrounding into the system.
Do not give a negative sign to an endothermic change; it is positive. Exothermic change is negative.
Do not treat heat and enthalpy as identical: heat is transferred energy, while enthalpy is thermal energy stored in a compound.
When describing a beaker example, do not name the beaker or burner as the water system; they are part of the surrounding.

explain.title: Enthalpy and its symbols
explain.body: “The total amount of heat energy present in a molecule under standard conditions (0°C temperature and 760 mm pressure) is also called its heat content. Enthalpy is the measurement of energy in a thermodynamic system. The quantity of enthalpy is equal to the total heat content of a system. Enthalpy of a system is represented by (H) while the change in enthalpy which a system undergoes is represented by ΔH.” In questions, keep H and ΔH distinct.

explain.title: What can be measured?
explain.body: “The total enthalpy (H) of a system cannot be measured directly. However, the change in enthalpy ΔH brought about in a system can be measured comparatively easily.” So chemistry questions usually compare the energy before and after a change.

explain.title: Standard enthalpy of reaction
explain.body: “In Chemistry, the standard enthalpy of reaction (ΔH°) is the enthalpy change when reactants in their standard states undergo reaction to produce products in their standard states.” It is also called the standard enthalpy change or heat of reaction at constant pressure.

explain.title: Heat compared with enthalpy
explain.body: “Heat is a form of energy that flows from hot body to a cold body because of a difference in temperature.” Enthalpy is part of a system and depends on its molecules, composition and structure. At constant pressure, enthalpy change equals the heat evolved or absorbed.

mistakes: Do not use H and ΔH as if they mean the same thing: H is enthalpy, while ΔH is its change.
Do not describe heat as energy stored in the system; heat is energy being transferred.

explain.title: Heat of a reaction
explain.body: Heat, which is evolved or absorbed during a chemical reaction, is called the heat of that reaction.

explain.title: Exothermic and endothermic reactions
explain.body: Chemical reactions in which heat energy is evolved are called exothermic reactions while those in which heat energy is absorbed are called endothermic reactions. Heat from an exothermic reaction goes to the surroundings and container, making them warmer. An endothermic reaction takes heat from the surroundings, so the container becomes cooler.

explain.title: The sign of ΔH
explain.body: When energy evolved is shown separately, an exothermic reaction has a negative ΔH. An endothermic reaction has a positive ΔH. Reversing a reaction reverses the direction of the heat change.

explain.title: Bond energy and the overall reaction
explain.body: Breaking bonds absorbs energy, while forming bonds evolves energy. The overall reaction is exothermic if more energy is released by bond formation than is absorbed in bond breaking. It is endothermic if more energy is absorbed than released.

explain.title: Exothermic reactions in everyday life
explain.body: Combustion of fuels releases heat used for cooking, heating and generating electricity. During metabolism, chemical energy in food is converted to heat. Fireworks are combustion reactions that produce heat, light and sound.

Do not assume that the reverse reaction has the same sign of ΔH; it has the opposite sign.

explain.title: Catalysts speed up reactions
explain.body: The textbook defines a catalyst as: “a substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction without itself undergoing any permanent chemical change.” A catalyst changes the path of the reaction and substantially decreases activation energy, so more reactants can form products.

notes.title: System, Surroundings and Energy Transfer
notes.answer: Heat energy moves from the surroundings into the water system; the change is endothermic.
notes.explanation: A system is the part of a change that we are studying. Everything outside it is the surrounding. Energy moving into the system makes the change endothermic; energy moving out of the system makes it exothermic.
notes.simple: The system is the part we are looking at. The surroundings are everything else. Heat going in means endothermic; heat going out means exothermic.
examples: When water boils in a beaker, the water is the system and the beaker and burner are part of the surrounding.
If a reaction releases heat to its surroundings, it is exothermic and has a negative enthalpy change.
steps: Identify the part being studied: this is the system.

If energy moves from the surrounding to the system, label the change endothermic and give it a positive sign.

notes.title: Enthalpy and heat
notes.answer: No. Only its enthalpy change, ΔH, can be measured comparatively easily.
notes.explanation: Enthalpy (H) is the total heat content of a system. We cannot measure H directly, but we can measure how much it changes, ΔH. Heat is energy being transferred from a hotter body to a colder body. At constant pressure, a system’s enthalpy change equals the heat it absorbs or releases.
notes.simple: Enthalpy is the energy content of a system. Heat is energy moving between bodies. We measure a change in enthalpy, not the system’s total enthalpy.
examples: For 2 CO(g) + O₂(g) → 2 CO₂(g), ΔH° = -566.0 kJ. The negative value means heat is released.
If a system absorbs heat at constant pressure, its enthalpy increases.
steps: Identify the system and its enthalpy, H.
Look at the enthalpy change, ΔH, rather than trying to measure H directly.
At constant pressure, use ΔH to describe the heat absorbed or released.
A negative ΔH means heat is released; a positive ΔH means heat is absorbed.
notes.checkQuestion: Can the total enthalpy of a system be measured directly?

notes.title: Exothermic and Endothermic Reactions
notes.answer: Exothermic reactions release heat; endothermic reactions absorb heat.
notes.explanation: Exothermic reactions release heat to the surroundings, while endothermic reactions absorb heat. Bond breaking absorbs energy; bond formation releases energy. To find the overall enthalpy change, add the energy used to break bonds to the energy released when new bonds form.
notes.simple: If a reaction gives heat out, it is exothermic. If it takes heat in, it is endothermic.
examples: When hydrogen and oxygen form water, heat is released: ΔH = −571.6 kJ for the reaction as written.
For H₂(g) + I₂(g) → 2HI(g), the bond-energy calculation using the values in Example 5.2 gives ΔH = 436 + 151 + 2(−299) = −11 kJ.
steps: Identify which bonds break and which bonds form.
Add the energies absorbed to break the bonds.
Add the energies released when the new bonds form, using negative values where given.
Add the two totals to find the enthalpy change, ΔH.
A negative ΔH means the reaction is exothermic; a positive ΔH means it is endothermic.

notes.title: How reactions take place
notes.answer: Reactant molecules collide. If they have enough energy, they can form a transition state, which may then form products.

Platinum acts as a catalyst in the production of H₂SO₄.

The transition state can change into products or return to reactants.
